quote: Only you can prevent forest fires.
speaker: Smokey Bear (original voice: Jackson Weaver)
source_title: Cooperative Forest Fire Prevention campaign, USDA Forest Service with the Ad Council
context_before: Radio and television spots, typically after a scene of a campfire left burning.
context_after: Campaign tag. In 2001 the wording changed to 'Only you can prevent wildfires' to reflect that some fire is ecologically useful.
cultural_background: Adopted as the campaign slogan in 1947, three years after Smokey was created in August 1944. It is one of the most recognised sentences in American life and the direct address to 'you' is the whole point of it.

licence_note: IMPORTANT TRAP: Smokey Bear looks federal but is NOT free. Unlike an ordinary red row, do not assume the slogan itself is free to re-voice for profit — check the statute's exact scope for Smokey before using the words at all.

L. 93-318, 1974) makes it a criminal offence to knowingly use, for profit, the Woodsy Owl character, the name, OR the slogan 'Give a Hoot, Don't Pollute' without Forest Service authorisation — fine or up to six months. The normal 'short phrases are not copyrightable, so re-voice it' workaround does NOT apply here: the statute reaches the words themselves. quote: This is your brain on drugs. Any questions?

cultural_background: Launched 1987 and drilled into a generation of American schoolchildren; TV Guide put it in the top hundred television advertisements ever made, Entertainment Weekly at number eight. Directed by Joe Pytka. 'Any questions?' is quoted in American speech independently of the ad.
why_it_lands: A complete argument made with kitchen equipment, ending with a rhetorical question that dares you to object. The structure is the comedy and it survives with no context — though Americans will also hear the whole 1980s in it.

quote: Just say no.
speaker: First Lady Nancy Reagan
source_title: Joint televised address on drug abuse from the West Hall of the White House
context_before: Nancy Reagan addressing children directly, near the end of the joint address.
context_after: An appeal to parents and to what she called a national crusade.
cultural_background: 14 September 1986, a rare joint address by a President and First Lady from the residence rather than the Oval Office. 'Just say no' became the name of an entire era of American drug policy and is now used mostly ironically, as shorthand for a slogan substituting for a policy.
why_it_lands: Three words offered as the answer to a national crisis. The gap between the scale of the problem and the size of the instruction is the joke, and it requires no American memory — though Americans hear a whole decade in it.
licence_note: Check this one carefully. The President's remarks in the same address are a US Government work under 17 U.S.C. 105. The First Lady is not a federal officer or employee, so section 105 does not clearly cover her portion — the point is unsettled and worth confirming before commercial use. The C-SPAN clip page is a locator only; source from the Reagan Library or the National Archives.

quote: Our job is never easy because drug criminals are ingenious.
speaker: First Lady Nancy Reagan
source_title: Joint televised address on drug abuse from the West Hall of the White House
context_before: Introducing the threat the campaign is aimed at.
context_after: 'They work every day to plot a new and better way to steal our children's lives, just as they've done by developing this new drug, crack.'
cultural_background: From the same 1986 address, and the sentence that introduced crack cocaine to much of the television audience. The framing — criminals as ingenious inventors with a product roadmap — set the tone of the decade's drug policy.
why_it_lands: 'Ingenious' is a compliment. The sentence accidentally admires the people it is condemning, in the flat cadence of an official address. Works standalone.
